stem: Conductive hearing loss occurs when sound transmission is disrupted between the external auditory canal and the inner ear, while which structures remain completely intact?
options: The tympanic membrane exclusively
The inner ear structures and the acoustic nerve
Only the ossicles
Only the Organ of Corti

stem: Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) results from damage to the cochlea, hair cells within the Organ of Corti, or which cranial nerve?
options: Cranial Nerve VII
Cranial Nerve VIII
Cranial Nerve IX
Cranial Nerve V

stem: In sensorineural hearing loss, sound transmission through the middle ear is unhindered, but which process is specifically impaired?
options: Neural conversion or transmission of sound
Cerumen production
Tympanic membrane vibration exclusively
Eustachian tube ventilation exclusively

stem: Mixed hearing loss is best described as:
options: A purely central auditory processing disorder with normal peripheral structures
A combination of conductive and sensorineural pathologies coexisting in the same ear
A condition exclusively affecting children
A condition that only affects one ear at a time by definition

stem: A patient with age-related nerve degeneration who ALSO develops a severe middle ear infection is a classic example of which type of hearing loss?
options: Pure conductive hearing loss
Pure sensorineural hearing loss
Mixed hearing loss
Functional/central hearing loss

stem: Functional (central) hearing loss is characterized by which combination of findings?
options: Damaged peripheral ear structures with normal central auditory processing
Normal peripheral ear structures but impaired central nervous system/auditory cortex processing of sound
Complete absence of the cochlea
Bilateral tympanic membrane perforation

stem: Which of the following is listed as a cause of CONDUCTIVE hearing loss specifically?
options: Presbycusis
Cerumen impaction or foreign bodies
Acoustic neuroma
Meniere's disease

stem: Otosclerosis, a recognized cause of conductive hearing loss, results specifically from which pathological process?
options: Degeneration of the Organ of Corti
Fixation of the stapes
Damage to Cranial Nerve VIII
Perforation of the round window

stem: Which of the following is listed as a cause of SENSORINEURAL hearing loss specifically?
options: Otitis media
Tympanic membrane perforation
Prolonged exposure to loud noise
Cerumen impaction

stem: Presbycusis is best described as:
options: A conductive hearing loss caused by cerumen accumulation
Age-related sensorineural degeneration
A form of central hearing loss exclusively
A reversible form of hearing loss caused by ear infection

stem: In a patient with CONDUCTIVE hearing loss, the Weber test will characteristically lateralize to which ear?
options: The unaffected (good) ear
The affected (bad) ear
Neither ear; it remains midline
Both ears equally, with no lateralization

stem: In a patient with SENSORINEURAL hearing loss, the Weber test will characteristically lateralize to which ear?
options: The affected (bad) ear
The unaffected (good) ear
It cannot lateralize in sensorineural loss
Both ears equally

stem: A NEGATIVE Rinne test result, where bone conduction is greater than or equal to air conduction (BC >= AC), is characteristic of which type of hearing loss?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss
Conductive hearing loss
Functional hearing loss
Normal hearing

stem: A POSITIVE Rinne test result in a patient with sensorineural hearing loss shows air conduction greater than bone conduction (AC > BC), but with which additional characteristic?
options: The overall time for both is normal and unremarkable
The overall time is reduced compared to a normal ear
Bone conduction is completely absent
Air conduction is completely absent

stem: Regarding reversibility, conductive hearing loss is generally described as:
options: Always permanent regardless of treatment
Often reversible with medical or surgical intervention
Only manageable with cochlear implants
Untreatable in all cases

stem: Regarding reversibility, sensorineural hearing loss is generally described as:
options: Typically permanent, managed with assistive devices
Always reversible with antibiotic therapy
Fully curable with tympanoplasty
Resolving spontaneously within weeks

stem: Nurses bear primary accountability for monitoring which specific adverse effect associated with certain high-risk medication classes affecting hearing?
options: Hepatotoxicity
Ototoxicity
Nephrotoxicity exclusively, with no ear-specific concern
Cardiotoxicity

stem: Which class of antibiotics is specifically listed as ototoxic, capable of permanently destroying cochlear hair cells?
options: Penicillins
Aminoglycosides
Macrolides
Tetracyclines

stem: Among the aminoglycosides listed as ototoxic, which of the following is included?
options: Amoxicillin
Gentamicin
Ciprofloxacin
Doxycycline

stem: Which class of diuretics is specifically noted to be highly ototoxic if infused too rapidly intravenously?
options: Thiazide diuretics
Potassium-sparing diuretics
Loop diuretics
Osmotic diuretics

stem: Furosemide, a loop diuretic listed as ototoxic, poses the greatest risk of ototoxicity under which specific administration condition?
options: When given orally over several days
When infused too rapidly intravenously
When given as a single low-dose tablet
When administered with food

stem: Which class of chemotherapeutic agents is specifically listed as ototoxic?
options: Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide
Platinum-based agents such as Cisplatin and Carboplatin
Antimetabolites such as methotrexate
Taxanes such as paclitaxel

stem: Chronic high-dose aspirin use, as an ototoxic agent, typically manifests with which characteristic and often REVERSIBLE symptom?
options: Permanent profound deafness
Tinnitus
Vertigo lasting for years
Complete loss of the vestibular reflex

stem: Which of the following is described as one of the common EARLY signs of hearing loss?
options: Complete inability to hear any sound at all
Frequently asking others to repeat themselves or stating that people are 'mumbling'
Sudden, complete deafness with no warning
Immediate need for a cochlear implant

stem: Inability to hear high-pitched sounds is described as the common FIRST sign of which specific condition?
options: Otitis media
Presbycusis
Cerumen impaction
Tympanic membrane perforation

stem: A patient with hearing loss may exhibit which characteristic change in their own speech pattern?
options: Speaking in an unusually loud or flat monotone voice
Speaking only in a whisper at all times
Complete loss of the ability to speak
Speaking exclusively in a high-pitched tone

stem: Social isolation resulting from unaddressed hearing loss is specifically linked to which secondary consequence?
options: Increased cognitive stimulation
Decreased cognitive stimulation
Improved mental health outcomes
Enhanced social engagement over time

stem: An emerging and critical link has been established between unaddressed hearing loss in older adults and which condition?
options: Accelerated cognitive decline
Improved memory retention
Decreased risk of dementia
Enhanced sensory integration

stem: When optimizing the environment for communicating with a hearing-impaired patient, the nurse should FIRST:
options: Turn on background music to create a calming atmosphere
Ensure the patient's full attention before speaking and minimize background noise
Begin speaking immediately regardless of the patient's attention
Increase the volume of the television to compensate

stem: When positioning to communicate with a hearing-impaired patient, the nurse should ensure the face is:
options: Turned away while speaking to avoid startling the patient
Well-lit and not in shadow, facing the patient directly
Partially covered by a hand while speaking
Positioned above the patient's line of sight only

stem: When communicating with a hearing-impaired patient, the nurse should specifically AVOID which behavior?
options: Facing the patient directly
Chewing gum or covering the mouth while speaking
Speaking at a natural pace
Using written instructions when needed

stem: When adjusting tone and pitch to communicate with a hearing-impaired patient, the nurse should NOT shout, primarily because shouting:
options: Lowers the pitch of the voice, making it easier to understand
Raises the pitch of the voice, making it harder to understand and distorting lip movements
Has no effect on pitch or lip movement at all
Only affects patients with conductive hearing loss, never sensorineural

stem: If a hearing-impaired patient does not understand a spoken phrase, the recommended nursing strategy is to:
options: Repeat the exact same phrase, only louder
Rephrase the sentence using simpler or different words
Write nothing down and simply gesture instead
Abandon the communication attempt entirely

stem: For conveying crucial educational information, such as medication timing, to a hearing-impaired patient, the nurse should utilize:
options: Only verbal communication at a louder volume
Visual supplements such as whiteboards, communication boards, or written instructions
Sign language only, without any visual aids
No supplementary aids, relying solely on lip reading

stem: When cleaning a patient's hearing aid, the nurse should use a dry, soft cloth and specifically avoid which practice?
options: Wiping the ear mold gently
Submerging the device in water or using harsh chemical solvents
Cleaning it once daily
Storing it in a labeled container

stem: At bedtime, when a hearing aid is not in use, the nurse should take which action to preserve battery life?
options: Leave the device on continuously
Turn it off and open the battery compartment
Submerge the battery compartment in water
Remove the battery and discard it immediately

stem: A high-pitched whistling noise (feedback) emitted from a patient's hearing aid while in the ear usually indicates which problem?
options: The battery is fully charged and functioning optimally
The ear mold is not inserted properly or is loose
The device requires no further attention
The patient's hearing has fully returned to normal

stem: For safe storage of a hearing aid not currently in use, the nurse should place it:
options: Loose on the patient's meal tray for easy access
In a labeled container inside the patient's bedside drawer
On the patient's bedsheets for convenience
Inside a tissue box at the bedside

stem: Storing a hearing aid loose on a meal tray, bedsheet, or tissue box poses which specific risk?
options: It will automatically recharge itself
It can easily be discarded accidentally
It will improve battery life
It has no associated risk

stem: Cochlear implants function by which mechanism?
options: Amplifying sound waves entering the external auditory canal only
Bypassing damaged hair cells in the cochlea to directly stimulate the auditory nerve
Reconstructing the tympanic membrane
Removing the stapes footplate

stem: Cochlear implants are indicated specifically for patients with which type and severity of hearing loss who derive no benefit from traditional hearing aids?
options: Mild unilateral conductive hearing loss
Profound, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Temporary conductive hearing loss from cerumen impaction
Functional hearing loss with normal peripheral structures

stem: Tympanoplasty is a surgical procedure aimed at which specific reconstruction?
options: Reconstruction of the cochlea
Reconstruction of the tympanic membrane to restore anatomy and improve conductive hearing
Reconstruction of the auditory cortex
Removal of the entire external ear

stem: Stapedectomy involves removal of the stapes footplate and insertion of which replacement structure?
options: A cochlear implant electrode array
A tissue graft or prosthesis
A hearing aid microphone
A tympanic membrane patch only, without prosthesis

stem: Stapedectomy is considered the gold standard surgical intervention for treating which specific condition?
options: Presbycusis
Otosclerosis
Acoustic neuroma
Meniere's disease

stem: Following ear surgery, the nurse should instruct the patient to avoid which specific action to prevent increased middle ear pressure?
options: Gentle chewing during meals
Blowing the nose forcefully, coughing, or sneezing with a closed mouth
Speaking in a normal conversational tone
Sitting upright in bed

stem: If a post-operative ear surgery patient must sneeze, the nurse should instruct them to:
options: Hold their breath and keep the mouth tightly closed
Keep their mouth open during the sneeze to avoid sudden pressure spikes in the middle ear
Pinch the nose shut while sneezing
Lie flat on the operative side during the sneeze

stem: Following ear surgery, the patient should be positioned with which ear facing down, to prevent pressure accumulation and graft displacement on the surgical side?
options: The affected (operated) ear
The unaffected (good) ear
Neither ear; the patient should remain supine at all times
It does not matter which side, as positioning has no effect

stem: Post-operative water precautions after ear surgery include keeping the ear dressing and canal dry, and during showers, using which specific protective measure in the outer ear?
options: A dry cotton ball only, with no additional barrier
A cotton ball saturated with petroleum jelly
A waterproof adhesive bandage placed directly over the ear canal opening
No protection is needed at any time

stem: Post-operative water precautions after ear surgery should be maintained until:
options: The patient feels ready to stop them, regardless of medical clearance
Cleared by the surgeon
Exactly 24 hours have passed, with no further individualization
The dressing falls off on its own

stem: Post-operatively, the nurse should monitor for severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, or sudden complete hearing loss, as these findings could indicate:
options: A normal, expected post-operative recovery pattern requiring no action
Inner ear injury or displacement of a prosthesis
Simple anesthesia-related nausea with no further significance
Improved surgical outcome

stem: According to the comparative table, the PRIMARY anatomical site involved in sensorineural hearing loss is the inner ear, cochlea, and:
options: The tympanic membrane
Cranial Nerve VIII
The external auditory canal
The ossicular chain exclusively

stem: Which condition is listed among the causes of sensorineural hearing loss, alongside Meniere's disease, involving a benign tumor affecting the vestibulocochlear nerve?
options: Otosclerosis
Acoustic neuroma
Otitis media
Tympanic membrane perforation

stem: A key distinguishing feature separating conductive from sensorineural hearing loss on the Weber test is that lateralization occurs to the BAD ear in conductive loss, whereas in sensorineural loss it lateralizes to the:
options: Same bad ear, identically to conductive loss
Good (unaffected) ear
Neither ear, remaining midline in both conditions
It cannot be tested in sensorineural loss at all

stem: Depression and mental fatigue in patients with hearing loss are specifically attributed to which mechanism, according to the psychosocial impact discussion?
options: Direct damage to mood-regulating brain centers by the hearing loss itself
The constant strain of trying to decode conversations
Medication side effects exclusively, unrelated to hearing status
Unrelated coincidental psychiatric comorbidity in all cases

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A patient undergoes Weber and Rinne testing. The Weber test lateralizes to the patient's LEFT ear, and the Rinne test on the left ear shows bone conduction greater than air conduction. These findings are MOST consistent with which diagnosis?
options: Sensorineural hearing loss in the left ear
Conductive hearing loss in the left ear
Normal hearing bilaterally
Sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear

stem: CASE SCENARIO (continued): Given this diagnosis, which of the following is the MOST likely underlying cause?
options: Presbycusis
Cerumen impaction or otosclerosis
Acoustic neuroma
Ototoxic medication use

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A different patient's Weber test lateralizes to the RIGHT ear, and Rinne testing on the LEFT ear shows air conduction greater than bone conduction, but with an overall reduced duration compared to normal. Which ear is affected, and by which type of hearing loss?
options: The right ear, with sensorineural hearing loss
The left ear, with sensorineural hearing loss
The left ear, with conductive hearing loss
The right ear, with conductive hearing loss

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A hospitalized patient is receiving IV gentamicin and IV furosemide concurrently for a severe infection with fluid overload. The nurse's PRIORITY concern related to hearing is:
options: Neither medication carries any ototoxic risk
The combined ototoxic risk of both medications, especially if furosemide is infused too rapidly
Only furosemide carries risk; gentamicin is completely safe for hearing
Only gentamicin carries risk; furosemide has no auditory effects

stem: CASE SCENARIO (continued): The nurse should specifically monitor this patient for which early warning signs of ototoxicity?
options: Improved hearing acuity and resolution of tinnitus
Tinnitus, vertigo, or new difficulty hearing
Increased appetite and improved mood
Decreased urine output exclusively, with no auditory relevance

stem: CASE SCENARIO: An elderly patient's family reports that he frequently asks people to repeat themselves, keeps the television volume very loud, and has started avoiding family gatherings. The nurse should recognize these findings as consistent with:
options: Normal age-related behavior requiring no further assessment
Early signs of hearing loss with psychosocial withdrawal
Definitive signs of dementia unrelated to hearing
A normal grief reaction requiring no intervention

stem: CASE SCENARIO (continued): The family also mentions he seems increasingly forgetful and less mentally sharp in recent months. The nurse understands this may reflect which established link discussed in the hearing loss literature?
options: A link between unaddressed hearing loss and accelerated cognitive decline
A completely unrelated coincidence with no evidence base
Definitive proof of early-stage Alzheimer's disease
A normal and reversible finding requiring no follow-up

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A nurse enters a hearing-impaired patient's room with the television on loudly and begins speaking to the patient from across the room while looking down at the chart. This approach violates several communication principles. Which correction should be made FIRST?
options: Speak even louder to compensate for the noise
Minimize background noise (turn off the TV) and ensure the patient's full attention before speaking
Continue as is, since the approach is already correct
Ask a family member to relay the message instead of engaging directly

stem: CASE SCENARIO (continued): When the patient still does not understand a particular phrase, the nurse should:
options: Repeat the identical phrase more loudly
Rephrase the sentence with simpler or different words
Give up and document that the patient is non-compliant
Shout the phrase directly into the patient's ear

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A patient's hearing aid is found lying loose on the bedside meal tray after breakfast. The nurse's BEST corrective action going forward is to:
options: Leave it there since it is convenient for the patient
Store it in a labeled container inside the bedside drawer when not in use
Place it inside the patient's water pitcher for safekeeping
Give it to a random visitor for safekeeping

stem: CASE SCENARIO (continued): The patient later reports the hearing aid is producing a high-pitched whistling sound while worn. The nurse's BEST initial action is to:
options: Assume the battery needs replacing without further assessment
Check that the ear mold is properly and snugly inserted
Discard the hearing aid immediately
Submerge the device in water to clean it

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A patient is 2 days post-stapedectomy and reports the urge to sneeze. The nurse should instruct the patient to:
options: Pinch the nose and close the mouth tightly during the sneeze
Keep the mouth open during the sneeze
Hold the sneeze in completely without any release
Lie flat on the operative ear during the sneeze

stem: CASE SCENARIO (continued): For post-operative positioning, the nurse should place this patient with which ear down?
options: The operated (surgical) ear
The unaffected (good) ear
Either ear, since positioning does not matter after stapedectomy
The patient should remain strictly upright at all times, never lying down

stem: CASE SCENARIO: On post-operative day 3 after tympanoplasty, a patient suddenly develops severe vertigo, nausea, and reports complete loss of hearing in the operated ear. The nurse's PRIORITY action is to:
options: Reassure the patient that this is an expected part of recovery and continue routine care

Administer an antiemetic only and defer further assessment until the next shift

stem: CASE SCENARIO: A patient with profound, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss has tried multiple hearing aids without any benefit. Which intervention is MOST appropriate for this patient?
options: A repeat trial of a different standard hearing aid
A cochlear implant
Tympanoplasty
Stapedectomy

stem: CASE SCENARIO (continued): The nurse explains to the patient's family that this device works by which mechanism, distinct from a conventional hearing aid?
options: It simply amplifies sound entering the ear canal, like a hearing aid
It bypasses the damaged hair cells and directly stimulates the auditory nerve

It replaces the stapes footplate with a prosthesis
